title: Google Cloud Moves the Compute Engine API to Immutable Date-Based Versions
gist: Google Cloud made multi-versioning of the Compute Engine API generally available: immutable, quarterly, date-stamped stable versions (starting 2026-09-01) and one-year -preview versions, selected via the X-Goog-Api-Version header or $apiVersion parameter, while the mutable /v1 surface stays with no end-of-life date. This lets Google change defaults, error formats and IAM checks for pinned callers without breaking /v1 automation, and makes Google the last of the three largest clouds to offer per-request API version pinning.

insights.claim: Google Cloud's Compute Engine API now offers immutable, date-stamped stable versions (named YYYY-MM-DD, released quarterly, starting with 2026-09-01) plus -preview versions with a one-year lifespan, alongside the long-lived /v1 surface.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Infrastructure-as-code and fleet automation on GCP now has an explicit pinning contract, lowering upgrade risk for large Compute Engine users.
insights.locator: Google Cloud has made multi-versioning of the Compute Engine API generally available

insights.claim: Compute Engine callers select a dated API version through the X-Goog-Api-Version header or the $apiVersion query parameter on the unchanged /compute/v1/ path, and requests naming no version keep getting /v1, which has no end-of-life date.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Opt-in design means no forced migration; adoption of new behavior will be gradual and driven by tooling defaults rather than customer action.
insights.locator: A caller selects one with the X-Goog-Api-Version header

insights.claim: Google moved Compute Engine to versioning because /v1 was a single mutable production surface shared by every customer worldwide, so any behavioral improvement risked breaking existing scripts or required multi-year migrations.
insights.speaker: Michael Murstein
insights.so_what: Signals Google is prioritizing the ability to modernize API behavior faster without breaking enterprise customers, a reliability lever in the cloud share fight.
insights.quote: was a single, mutable production surface shared by every customer worldwide
insights.locator: Software engineer Michael Murstein writes that the problem was the shape of /v1 itself

insights.claim: Each stable Compute Engine date version is a locked snapshot of all generally available features and defaults at that date with no breaking changes after publication, following Google's AIP-185 which requires stable versions to be dates and previews to be time-bound.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: AIP-185 interface-based versioning is a template Google may extend to other APIs; watch for adoption beyond Compute Engine.
insights.locator: Google calls the replacement interface-based versioning

insights.claim: In Compute Engine's date-based API versions, AggregatedList returns partial results by default (in /v1 only when returnPartialSuccess is set), so one failing zone no longer fails a fleet-wide query.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Improves resilience of fleet-wide tooling on GCP; operators should audit code that assumed all-or-nothing list semantics before pinning.
insights.quote: so one failing zone no longer fails a fleet-wide query
insights.locator: A default: /v1 returns partial results from AggregatedList

insights.claim: New Compute Engine API versions return structured google.rpc.ErrorInfo error bodies with reason, domain and metadata, and requesting a nonexistent version returns metadata listing the versions that do exist.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Error-parsing code in automation will need updating when moving off /v1.
insights.locator: The error body, which becomes structured google.rpc.ErrorInfo

insights.claim: Date-based versions let Compute Engine tighten overly broad legacy IAM permission checks, introduce safer configuration defaults and migrate decade-old resource schemas toward Google's API Improvement Proposals, while automation pinned to /v1 sees none of these changes.
insights.speaker: Michael Murstein
insights.so_what: Security posture improvements on GCP will accrue only to callers on new versions, creating a security gap for /v1-pinned estates.
insights.quote: tighten overly broad legacy IAM permission checks and introduce safer configuration defaults
insights.locator: Permissions. Murstein says new versions let Compute Engine

insights.claim: Most Compute Engine callers will adopt dated API versions through tooling: each client library release for Python, Go, Java, Node.js, C#, Ruby and PHP binds to one date-based version without changing compute_v1/apiv1 import paths, gcloud compute targets the bundled stable version, and the Terraform google provider targets stable while google-beta targets preview.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Behavior changes will reach users silently through routine SDK/Terraform upgrades, so pinning library versions becomes the effective API-version control.
insights.quote: Most callers will meet the change through tooling rather than headers.
insights.locator: Most callers will meet the change through tooling rather than headers

insights.claim: With Compute Engine multi-versioning, Google is the last of the three largest cloud providers to let callers pin an API version on a request: Azure Resource Manager has required a date-stamped api-version parameter since launch, while AWS keeps date-stamped service models inside its SDKs and exposes no per-request version selection.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Google is catching up to Azure on API stability conventions; AWS now stands out as the hyperscaler without per-request version pinning.
insights.locator: With this release, Google is the last of the three largest cloud providers

insights.claim: Google's header-based versioning follows the pattern Stripe popularized (Stripe-Version header, e.g. 2026-10-28.endive, with monthly non-breaking releases and twice-yearly major releases that may break), but unlike Stripe Google has not said which quarterly versions will carry breaking changes.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Stripe's model has become the reference for API evolution; ambiguity over Google's breaking-change cadence is a planning risk for platform teams.
insights.locator: The header form Google chose is the one Stripe popularized

insights.claim: Google has given no end-of-life date for Compute Engine /v1, no path for a preview version to become stable, no complete list of /v1 vs 2026-09-01 behavioral differences, no statement on other Google Cloud APIs adopting the scheme, and no mention of the /beta and /alpha channels.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Watch for follow-on announcements extending date-versioning to other GCP APIs or a /v1 deprecation timeline, either of which would force customer migration work.
insights.locator: Google gives no end-of-life date for /v1
